newsitem.title: CHINA: Calif. pensions look to private China investments.
newsitem.headline: Calif. pensions look to private China investments.

text.p: Managers from California's main pension funds said on Tuesday the Shanghai stock exchange was too immature to consider for investment and that they were looking at investing in China through private equity deals.
But they said they were amazed by the rate of growth in China's largest industrial city, and saw a gradual shift in the portfolios under their control in this direction.

The public pension fund managers, led by California State Treasurer Matt Fong, are on an eight-day Asian tour to investigate investment possibilities. They met Shanghai's mayor Xu Kuangdi during a one-day visit to the city.

"I have never seen an area of growth like Shanghai in all my life," said Thomas Flanagan, chief investment officer with the California State Teachers Retirement System which controls $65 billion in funds.
"We recognise there are risks, but we have the word of the mayor that we won't lose money (by investing here)," he said.

But William Crist, board president of the California Public Employees' Retirement System, the largest of the U.S. pension funds with $105 billion, said the foreign currency B shares on the Shanghai stock exchange could not be considered at present.
"The amount of transparency that we would expect with the companies is not available at this point," he said.
Patricia Small, treasurer of the University of California, said the highly speculative trading in B shares by domestic Chinese investors also made foreign pension fund managers wary.
"That's why we went the private equity route," she said.

Several of the managers said they had made private investments in smaller Chinese companies as an alternative to public equity investment, and said they would continue to prefer this method of investing in China.
"We have decided that we can't wait for the Shanghai Stock Exchange to mature, and we are looking for other investment vehicles," said Crist.
The seven pension funds represented in the delegation control a total of $234 billion in funds.
